newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks buck Wall St., pulled up by Telmex.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks buck Wall St., pulled up by Telmex.

text.p: Mexican stocks closed higher Tuesday as gains in heavyweight Telmex offset a falling Dow Jones industrial average and higher U.S. long-bond yields.
"The market's dead, and gains in Telmex, which accounted for one-third of shares traded today, hauled the market up from an earlier slump," a trader said.
The blue-chip IPC index closed the year at 3,361.03 points, 14.08 points or 0.42 percent up on the day, but up 582.56 points, or 20.97 percent from the close of 1995.
Volume was a moribund 30.2 million shares traded, due to the absence of foreign players, a trader said.

The Dow Jones plummeted 101.10 points, or 1.54 percent to 6,448.27 points. Yields on 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds were up to 6.64 percent, from 6.55 percent in late trade Monday as the long bond fell more than 1-1/4 points.
Telmex "L" series shares closed up eight centavos (1 cent) to 12.98 pesos ($1.64) in Mexico, while its ADRs went against the tide in the New York to gain 1/8 to 33.

Traders noted Telmex stock was in demand by the Inbursa brokerage, which has corporate links to the firm. They thus suspected gains were for year-end valuation purposes rather than betokening any fundamental trend.
"I thought they'd try to get it up to $33 to close the year, and they did," one dealer said, referring to Telmex ADRs.
On the broad market 103 stocks were traded, of which 61 were up while 31 fell.
Dealers said stocks heading the gainers' list were mostly purchases to register prices to close portfolios for the year.
Debt ridden holding company Sidek gained most in percentage terms, up 20 centavos (3 cents) to 1.20 pesos (15 cents), but still well down from its 1996 high of 4.30 pesos (54 cents).
Financial group Abaco series "A" and "B" series shares headed the sliders, down 41 centavos (5 cents) and 30 centavos (4 cents), respectively, at 2.39 (30 cents) and 2.15 pesos (27 cents).
Dealers said financial stocks in general had been hit by the impending introduction of accountancy guidelines more in line with international criteria.
The new guidelines would effectively increase many banks' estimates of their sizeable past-due loans burdens and thus force them to create greater reserves.
